title: Hermitian Symmetric Spaces
notes: Open by telling students that this chapter is a bridge, not a catalog. The left side is local complex geometry: an operator J, type splitting, Kahler metrics, and Ricci curvature. The right side is global symmetric-space structure: an isotropy center, Bergman metrics, and a bounded realization in p minus coordinates.

title: The Chapter Moves Through Five Gates
notes: Use the roadmap to prevent the chapter from feeling like five unrelated topics. Each gate preserves an invariant that will be used later. Type splitting controls tensor formulas, the Kahler condition controls curvature, Bergman kernels make bounded domains metric spaces, the center of K recognizes Hermitian type, and the final representation turns the structure into coordinates.

title: The First Test Is Algebraic
notes: Slow down on the difference between algebra and geometry. The equation J squared equals minus identity is checked independently at every tangent space, so it is local linear algebra. Integrability is stronger: it asks whether those tangent rotations can be coordinated by complex charts. That distinction matters because symmetric-space arguments first build an invariant J and then verify that it is compatible with the geometry.

title: Complexifying The Tangent Bundle Splits The Problem
notes: The type split is the chapter's first piece of reusable bookkeeping. Once the tangent bundle is complexified, J has two eigenbundles, and the projection formulas make that split calculable. Students should hear that the formulas are not cosmetic: they are how tensor statements later separate into same-type and mixed-type blocks.

title: Compatibility Turns Tensor Calculations Into Block Patterns
notes: Treat this slide as a visual substitute for a long index calculation. The Hermitian metric does not pair two holomorphic directions or two antiholomorphic directions; it pairs opposite types. The Kahler condition says the connection preserves J, so this type discipline survives differentiation and curvature operations instead of being a one-time coordinate trick.

title: The Bergman Kernel Produces A Kahler Metric
notes: Connect this calculation to the later domain theorem. The Bergman kernel is not just an analytic object; differentiating its logarithm gives the metric that bounded domains naturally carry. In the disk model students can see two facts at once: the metric becomes large near the boundary, and the Ricci expression is locked to the metric by a simple symbolic identity.

title: Disk Symmetries Model The General Definition
notes: Use the disk as a controlled laboratory for the definition. A bounded symmetric domain asks for a holomorphic involution centered at every point, with that point isolated as a fixed point. In the disk, the fractional linear formula makes each obligation visible, and the Bergman metric supplies the invariant geometry that will generalize.

title: Symmetry Must Preserve The Complex Structure
notes: This is the conceptual definition slide. A symmetric space already has geodesic symmetries, but the Hermitian adjective requires the complex structure to be part of the invariant geometry. The point for students is that J is not an arbitrary decoration on the manifold; it is respected by the same symmetry group that controls geodesics and curvature.

title: The Center Of The Isotropy Group Supplies J
notes: Present the center criterion as the practical fingerprint of Hermitian type. Instead of searching for complex coordinates directly, one looks at the isotropy action. A central circle rotates every tangent complex line, and its derivative gives the operator J. Centrality is what makes the construction invariant rather than dependent on a chosen tangent vector.

title: The Same Hermitian Algebra Has Two Curvature Faces
notes: This slide keeps the compact and noncompact stories from splitting into two unrelated lectures. The algebraic recognition test is shared: an isotropy center acts as the complex structure. What changes is the global curvature and coordinate behavior. The noncompact side is the one that will be realized as a bounded domain, while the compact dual supplies the comparison geometry.

title: A Bounded Symmetric Domain Carries Its Own Geometry
notes: Frame this direction as the analytic-to-geometric theorem. A bounded symmetric domain begins as a complex domain with holomorphic point symmetries. The Bergman kernel manufactures a canonical Kahler metric, and the transformation law makes automorphisms isometries. From there the domain is not just an example; it becomes a Hermitian symmetric space of noncompact type.

title: The Noncompact Space Enters A Bounded Vector Domain
notes: This is the algebraic heart of the final section. The theorem does not draw the bounded domain by guessing coordinates; it embeds the noncompact symmetric space into a complexified group picture and then reads off the P minus factor. The message is that boundedness comes from the Lie-theoretic factorization plus the Hermitian type decomposition.

title: Strongly Orthogonal Directions Reveal Boundedness
notes: Use this slide to make the boundedness theorem feel inspectable. The full proof uses strongly orthogonal roots and the complexified group, but the coordinate behavior has a simple numerical fingerprint: real geodesic coordinates are sent through tanh. That is why unbounded motion in the symmetric space can land inside a bounded coordinate domain.

title: Each Ingredient Feeds The Bounded-Domain Theorem
notes: Use this as a synthesis slide before the final checklist. The arrows encode the teaching logic: local complex algebra creates type splitting; type splitting makes the Kahler and Ricci formulas meaningful; isotropy center data recognizes Hermitian symmetric spaces; Bergman geometry handles bounded domains; and the Cartan-Harish-Chandra map closes the loop from Lie theory back to a bounded complex domain.

title: How To Recognize The Chapter In A New Example
notes: Close by turning the lecture into a reusable diagnostic. Given a new symmetric-space example, students should not start by memorizing its classification label. They should ask for the operator J, its type split, the Hermitian metric blocks, the isotropy center, and finally the bounded-domain coordinate behavior. That workflow is the chapter's durable skill.
